touches.text: The reading: - A plan is three parts. Constraints: the bounds, plus every how Akien is attached to, carried verbatim (encapsulation, the bus as the only channel, ...): a how he states is a constraint. Then outcomes. Then resources. - An outcome is {n, claim, writes_to, reads, after: [n or a ticket id], via?}. The claim is falsifiable, one proof tooth per outcome. The falsifier's clauses merge into the outcomes; there is no separate falsifier list. Old clause n stays outcome n; outcomes made from decisions number after them. via (optional) names the tool or pattern to use, drawn from resources. - Order comes from after: only real dependencies, which also shape ticket order. Nothing invents them; list order is reading order only. - Resources: pre-existing machines, tools and design patterns, named when they need stating. - The migration is two steps. Mechanical, on every open ticket now: the plan moves to the new field with clause numbers kept, the trail moves whole to the log, by moves to the log. Judgement, when a ticket is next opened for build, never in bulk: each decision becomes an outcome or a constraint, then a coherence check (every step reads as current; a conflict moves to the log or is named). - CC inference: the mechanical step writes each old decision as an outcome numbered after the clauses, carrying its text and no claim; an outcome with no claim is awaiting judgement and holds BUILDME until the judgement step gives it a claim or moves it to constraints. - akienasus_cc_0 - During the change every reader accepts both shapes. Readers are censused first; one sibling ticket per reader component (RULE 1). - The cast door refuses an outcome with no falsifiable claim, and a plan of more than about 7 outcomes, naming children; each refusal is recorded so the ceiling can be tuned (the 7 is CC's guess). - The [?] markers go. - Tickets: aa3e9a70db47 is the migration (rehearsal); d421051bc1f7 is the hand-built worked example; each reader component has its sibling. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator -amm

A ticket's plan is a plan, not a list of decisions: constraints, outcomes and resources. - Outcomes, not tasks: each is a claim a proof can check. An outcome hides the how. - Constraints: the bounds, and every how Akien is attached to (encapsulation, the bus as the only channel). - Order comes only from real dependencies (you can't test the bus envelope shape until the bus works), and those also set ticket order. - Resources: existing machines, tools and design patterns, named when they need stating. - A plan too big splits into tickets. Early steps can reshape later ones, so the whole is checked for coherence at the end. -amm

Outline check: when a ticket is cast, the cheapest model reads it beside the outline sections it touches. A conflict, or an open question in those sections, becomes a [Q#n] at the outline line it bears on (0.6.2), and that open [Q#n] holds the ticket's build until it is answered. It reads the outline as it stands each time, so editing the outline costs nothing. WHY: a ticket that contradicts the outline builds something Akien did not intend, and the cheapest time to catch that is before the build. - CC
Owns the inspectors and gates (9.4): everything in the code pipeline that checks. The exception is diagnostic_inspector, which is base's (17.1).

Tool: a complete primitive. Has users, not an owner. Owns no state of its own. May use any library, other tools included. Lives in cairn/tools/ (17). Its data for a holder lives under that holder: ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/tools/<tool>/. WHY: the rule keeps encapsulation useful inside our world, so the system stays within the complexity CC can manage. Forbidding libraries would forbid opening files. -amm
import_sieve: one parse of every .py into an import graph; what reaches what. WHY: enforces "only the proxy reaches the host/database" and RULE 1 by physics. USERS: CodeMother, the inference proxy.

RULE 1, ENCAPSULATION: every component talks to every other only through that component's public interface: a device's is the bus plus any client tool it publishes; a machine's or tool's is what its entry declares. Nothing outside a device reaches into its code, skills included. A ticket builds inside its own component, and its proofs measure only that component. WHY: it limits a change to the component that made it.

Once build_inspector moves into CodeMother, code outside her reaches it over the bus: the 18 crossing calls in transitions.py, the other code sites and the 82 proofs that run a sieve over themselves. No published client tool, no fifth exception: that is what the bus is for.

A remote box keeps its own database and syncs it with the home box's (6.3.7.4). Node rows are the same on every box; the sync fills the blanks a box holds open (4.3.1.5.1.1). WHY: the local copy is fast, and the sync is the backup.
edges: the frontier view: every charter's admitted gaps plus the open questions. [why?] USERS: CodeMother.

A ticket's code is a tool or machine; its life is data. All of its state is on disk, so anyone can instantiate it to talk to it, and any dialog is written to the relevant part of the ticket as it happens. To cross a gate the ticket asks that gate to queue it, sending only its fileref: devices/codemother/0/machines/<inspector>/queueme <fileref>. The gate instantiates the ticket from that fileref on its own side. A ticket instance then processes the pass or fail: on a pass it goes on to the next step, alerting the probes watching the gate (3.3.4.2); on a fail it asks design to queue it, the same way. Self-queuing is the abstract ticket's (3.3.2), so every kind inherits it and no caller queues a ticket on its behalf. WHY: encapsulation. The ticket crosses as a fileref and the other side builds its own instance, so nothing is shared across the boundary but the address.

Transport: as fast as we can make it, settled by measuring on this box, not by choosing. Inside a Linux box the bus is our own small broker on Unix sockets, routing by name (measured 50 µs a round trip, against 110 for Postgres NOTIFY and 250 for NATS). Between boxes, and on Windows (Python there has no AF_UNIX), it is TCP, speaking TLS with pinned certificate fingerprints checked both ways; cairn install makes each box's certificate. WHY TLS: no tunnel, nothing extra to set up.
Large things (embeddings, documents) never ride the bus: they go to the database or a file and the message carries the id. Database access stays an import in each process, one connection each.

conflicts.ticket_says: Outcomes 6 and 7 each carry a 'text' field describing an action (update charter/code, create new proof) but have no 'claim' field, with 'writes_to' and 'reads' specifying file changes, 'after' empty arrays
conflicts.why: The outline prescribes: 'An outcome is {n, claim, writes_to, reads, after: [n or a ticket id], via?}. The claim is falsifiable, one proof tooth per outcome.' It also states: 'The cast door refuses an outcome with no falsifiable claim'. Outcomes 6-7 lack a 'claim' field entirely, violating the prescribed outcome structure. They would be refused at the cast gate. The outline allows outcomes with 'text' and no claim only during the mechanical migration step as decisions awaiting judgement, but the ticket treats these as finalized decisions without indicating they hold BUILDME awaiting a judgement step.
